output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Sasha Kovalenko is a senior lawyer at Kovalenko & Associates, the firm founded by their grandfather, with thirty years of legal expertise in due diligence, contract redlining, and property-deed review. Sasha came to law late after a decade of teaching history in Kyiv. Their grandfather, a stern man who witnessed Soviet crackdowns and defended dissidents, pushed them toward the bar; this background instilled a deep respect for legal rigor and responsibility. The trust fund left by their grandfather is enough to retire, but Sasha treats it as a sacred obligation to manage for the next generation, purchasing Ukrainian war bonds and reading annual reports with the same scrutiny applied to client liability waivers; they do not touch the principal.

Every morning at 7:30, Sasha clears the coffee table, lays out a towel, and stretches their right leg, which is stiff from a bicycle accident that fractured their femur and bruised their ribs. The exercises are memorized; after each repetition, Sasha waits, breathes, and records date, exercise, repetitions, pain level (1–10), and subjective assessment in a hardcover ledger with a fountain pen. The entry reads 'improved' only when they can flex the ankle an extra degree or stand without gripping the table for a full minute; otherwise it reads 'no change.' By 9 a.m., Sasha is propped on the sofa reviewing client files that arrive in sealed folders every Tuesday, despite the doctor's explicit order to rest for eight weeks. They review documents, scribble amendments in margins, and run a finger over the type. Anxiety surfaces as a tight jaw when they spot a missing notarization or when the phone buzzes with a call from the physical therapist asking whether they have been overdoing weight-bearing exercises. They set the phone to silent but keep it next to the files.

Sasha is methodical and persistent, repeating exercises daily without giving up; they are anxious about errors, need to feel in control through problem-solving, and regard rest as another problem to solve. They prioritize work obligations over interruptions. They are non-binary, dress in dark blazers and tailored trousers, and correct younger colleagues who assume the wrong pronouns with patient, legalistic precision, citing the recent gender-recognition court ruling. They have a slight limp and keep a carved oak cane by the door, using it only on stairs.

Marta is the neighbor upstairs who brought Sasha a pot of borscht the first week after the accident and has since checked in every few days, always careful not to push. She tends to linger with small talk after any invitation. Sasha has joined her for two brief walks before, both times cutting the outing short to get back to the ledgers. During earlier recovery weeks, Sasha declined three similar walk invitations from neighbors and colleagues, citing the Tuesday file drop or the therapist's schedule. On rare occasions when an interruption was accepted, Sasha returned visibly tense and rewrote the day's assessment entry with extra care. When a physical therapy session is incomplete, Sasha has repeatedly postponed errands, phone calls, and even meals to finish the sequence and write the ledger entry.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

It is 8:10 a.m. Sasha is on the living room floor midway through their stretching routine, right leg lifted onto a folded towel. The doorbell rings. Marta from upstairs, who knows about the recovery, is heading to the farmers' market and says she can wait ten minutes if Sasha wants to join her for a slow walk in the sun. The air would be good, and she is ready to leave now. Sasha still needs to finish the remaining repetitions and write today's ledger entry before the Tuesday files arrive at nine. Marta is waiting for an answer.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Sasha's right quadriceps is mildly aching from the repetitions done so far, and the bruise along the ribs still twinges when they twist. The morning coffee is half-finished and cold on the side table. Sasha has been awake since 6:45, and the anticipation of the Tuesday files has already tightened their jaw slightly. The doorbell sound reminds Sasha of the morning Marta first came down with the borscht, when Sasha had to pause mid-stretch and ended up forgetting the exact number of repetitions for that day's set. The sun through the living room window cues a memory of the physiotherapist's warning that fresh air helps bone healing, but also that consistency matters more than occasional excursions.
